rw: Utilities and rent are ongoing costs of running the store that do not depend on how much is sold, which is exactly what overhead means for a retailer.

ww.The cost of goods sold: Cost of goods sold is a direct cost tied to the products sold, not an overhead cost that stays fixed regardless of sales volume.
ww.Commissions on sales: Commissions on sales vary with how much is sold, so they are a variable selling cost rather than a fixed overhead expense for the store.
ww.The price buyers pay: The price buyers pay is the store's revenue, which is money coming in, so it cannot be a cost the store carries as overhead.

rw: Operating profit is revenue minus cost of goods sold minus operating expenses, so 500,000 minus 300,000 minus 120,000 leaves 80,000 for the business.

ww.$920,000: The figure 920,000 comes from adding all three numbers together, but costs must be subtracted from revenue, not added to it, so this is wrong.
ww.$380,000: The figure 380,000 is revenue minus operating expenses only, which forgets to subtract the 300,000 cost of goods sold from the 500,000 revenue figure.
ww.$200,000: The figure 200,000 is revenue minus cost of goods sold only, which is gross profit, and it ignores the 120,000 of operating expenses still to deduct.

rw: A business takes in inputs such as labor, materials and capital and transforms them into goods or services that customers value enough to pay for.

ww.Stores them without ever using them in c: Hoarding resources unused earns nothing and wastes them, so it is not what a business does; businesses use inputs to produce something customers will pay for.
ww.Burns them to heat the factory in the wi: Burning resources for heat is not the purpose of taking them in; a business converts inputs into output it can sell, not simply consumes them as fuel.
ww.Gives them away to competitors for no pa: Giving resources to competitors for nothing would destroy value and profit, and it is the opposite of how a business turns inputs into sellable products.

rw: A limited partnership has at least one general partner with full liability and one or more limited partners whose liability stops at what they invested in the firm.

ww.A partnership where no one is ever liabl: If no partner were ever liable for the firm's debts, that would describe a corporation style shield for everyone, whereas a limited partnership still needs at least one liable partner.
ww.A partnership with no profit sharing amo: Profit sharing is normal in a limited partnership because partners agree how profits are divided, so a partnership with no sharing does not describe this form at all.
ww.A partnership limited to two people and: Limiting a partnership to two people is not what makes it limited; the word refers to limited liability for some partners, and any number of partners may join.

rw: In a general partnership all partners share in managing the business and all carry unlimited personal liability for its debts, which is what makes it general.

ww.A partnership where one partner is liabl: In a general partnership every partner is personally liable for firm debts, not just one, so a single liable partner describes a limited partnership structure instead.
ww.A partnership run by the government of t: A general partnership is a private business owned by its partners, not a government body, and nothing about it involves running a state operation for the public.
ww.A partnership with shareholders who vote: Shareholders who vote on every decision belong to a corporation; a general partnership has partners, not shareholders, and partners manage the firm directly themselves.

rw: A partnership agreement is a written contract that sets out each partner's duties, share of profits and losses, and rights, so disputes can be settled by its terms.

ww.A loan from a bank to a partner to fund: A loan from a bank is a financing contract between the lender and borrower; a partnership agreement is instead a contract among the partners themselves about running the firm.
ww.A tax form filed with the state, listing: A tax form listing partner profits is a filing made with the government after the year ends, while the partnership agreement is a private contract made among the partners.
ww.A license to sell goods in the town, iss: A license to sell goods in town is a permit issued by a city authority, which is a different document from the agreement signed privately among the partners.

rw: Partners can disagree over decisions, and in a general partnership each partner can be held liable for debts and acts of the other partners, which is a real weakness.

ww.It pays no taxes at all in any year on i: Partnerships do pay tax on profits through the partners' personal returns, so the claim that they pay no taxes at all in any year is false.
ww.It cannot raise any money from partners: Partnerships can raise money from partners' contributions and from lenders, though often less than corporations can, so saying they cannot raise any money is an overstatement.
ww.It must be run by a single person, who d: A partnership has two or more owners by definition, so being run by a single person who decides for all partners describes a sole proprietorship, not a partnership.

rw: Double taxation happens when a corporation pays tax on its profits and shareholders then pay tax again on the dividends received from those same after tax profits.

ww.Paying sales tax at two different stores: Paying sales tax at two stores covers two separate purchases, each taxed once, which is not double taxation; the term refers to the same income taxed twice.
ww.Paying tax twice on a purchase made in o: Paying tax twice on one purchase at one store does not happen under normal sales tax rules, and double taxation is about corporate profits and dividends instead.
ww.Filing two tax returns in one year, stat: Filing both state and federal returns means two different governments each tax income once, so it is not double taxation, which taxes the same corporate profit twice.

rw: An S corporation passes its income, losses and credits through to its owners, who report them on their personal returns, which avoids the corporate level of tax.

ww.A corporation that never pays tax to any: An S corporation is still subject to tax rules because its owners pay income tax on their shares, so saying it never pays tax to any government is false.
ww.A corporation owned by the state and run: State ownership describes a government enterprise, whereas an S corporation is privately owned by shareholders and is defined by its special pass through tax status.
ww.A corporation formed only abroad in a fo: An S corporation is a United States tax designation for domestic firms, not a company formed abroad, and it is defined by pass through taxation instead.

rw: A board of directors is a group elected by shareholders to oversee a corporation's management, set major goals and hire or replace the senior executives of the firm.

ww.The employees of a corporation who work: Employees who work for the corporation each day are the staff, not the board; the board is a group chosen to oversee the top managers of the firm.
ww.Customers who buy company stock in the o: Customers who buy stock in the open market become shareholders, and only the shareholders elect the board, so customers as a group are not the board.
ww.A bank that lends to the company and set: A bank that lends to the company is a creditor, not a board; the board of directors is elected by shareholders to guide and oversee management.

rw: A shareholder owns shares of stock in a corporation, which gives a share of ownership, a claim on profits through dividends, and usually a vote on key matters.

ww.A supplier of raw materials to firms: A supplier of raw materials sells inputs to firms and is a vendor, while a shareholder owns a piece of the company through its shares of stock.
ww.A lender who holds the company's loans: A lender holding the company's loans is a creditor who is owed repayment, whereas a shareholder is an owner with a claim on profits and assets.
ww.A worker paid by the hour at a firm: A worker paid by the hour is an employee earning wages, which does not make that person an owner; shareholders hold stock and are the owners.

rw: A stakeholder is anyone affected by or with an interest in a business's decisions, including employees, customers, suppliers, owners and the local community around it.

ww.Only the owners of the business itself: Owners are only one group of stakeholders; the term is wider and also covers employees, customers, suppliers and communities who are affected by what a business does.
ww.Only the competitors of the business as: Competitors may be affected by a business, but they are only one kind of stakeholder, and the term is far broader than rivals alone.
ww.Only the managers of the business itself: Managers are stakeholders but not the only ones, since employees, customers, suppliers, owners and communities are also affected by the firm's decisions and actions.

rw: Vertical integration means a firm owns several stages of its supply chain, such as supplying inputs, making the product and selling it directly to customers.

ww.A firm selling to many countries around: Selling to many countries is international expansion, which concerns where a firm sells, not whether it owns more than one stage of its supply chain.
ww.A firm splitting into smaller units over: A firm splitting into smaller units is a breakup or spin off, which is the reverse of integrating stages of production under one owner.
ww.Two rivals merging at the same stage of: Two rivals merging at the same stage of production is horizontal integration, whereas vertical integration joins different stages of the supply chain under one owner.

rw: Horizontal integration is when a firm merges with or buys a competitor operating at the same stage of production, which raises market share and cuts duplicate costs.

ww.Selling part of the company to new outsi: Selling part of the company to outside investors raises capital and changes ownership, but it does not combine firms at the same stage of production.
ww.Opening a store in a new country on anot: Opening a store in a new country is geographic expansion, which does not involve merging with a competitor at the same stage of the supply chain.
ww.Buying a supplier of raw materials to co: Buying a supplier of raw materials to control early steps is vertical integration, since it moves backward along the supply chain rather than across to a competitor.

rw: A merger is when two companies agree to combine into a single new or surviving firm, usually to gain scale, share markets or reduce costs.

ww.A company paying a dividend out: A company paying a dividend simply distributes part of its profit to shareholders, and nothing is combined with another company in that event.
ww.A company closing its doors for good: A company closing its doors is a shutdown or liquidation, which ends the business instead of joining it with another firm as a merger does.
ww.One company splitting into two firms: One company splitting into two firms is a breakup or spin off, which is the opposite of a merger, where two firms join to form one.

rw: An acquisition occurs when one company buys enough of another to take control of it, and the target usually becomes part of the buyer or its subsidiary.

ww.A firm hiring a new CEO for the job: Hiring a new CEO is a management change inside one firm and does not transfer control of the company to another firm as an acquisition does.
ww.A firm closing a branch in another city: Closing a branch is a cost cutting or restructuring step within one company, and no other company gains control of it, so it is not an acquisition.
ww.Two firms agreeing to share a logo: Two firms sharing a logo might be a branding or licensing deal, but neither firm buys control of the other, so it is not an acquisition.

rw: A hostile takeover is an acquisition that the target company's management opposes, so the buyer goes straight to shareholders or buys up shares to win control.

ww.A strike by employees against the compan: A strike by employees is a labor dispute between workers and owners and has nothing to do with another company buying control of the target.
ww.A theft of company property by a group o: Theft of company property by staff is a crime committed inside the firm and is unrelated to one company seeking to take over another firm.
ww.An acquisition both sides welcome, with: An acquisition that both sides welcome with managers in favor is a friendly takeover, which is the opposite of a hostile one.

rw: The executive summary is a short overview of the whole business plan, placed first, that gives readers the key points such as the idea, market and financial needs.

ww.A list of every employee's pay: A list of every employee's pay would be part of a detailed payroll or staffing section, not a short summary that introduces the whole business plan.
ww.A legal contract with investors: A legal contract with investors is a separate document, such as an investment agreement, and an executive summary is only a summary of the plan itself.
ww.A full set of financial statements: A full set of financial statements is a long, detailed section of the plan, whereas the executive summary is brief and only highlights the main financial points.

rw: A franchisee is a person or firm that buys the right to run a business under an established brand, paying fees and following the franchisor's methods.

ww.The company that owns the brand and lice: The company that owns the brand and licenses it to others is the franchisor, not the franchisee, who is the person buying the right to use that brand.
ww.A supplier of the brand's goods and mate: A supplier of goods and materials sells products to outlets, which is a vendor role, while a franchisee is the person who runs a branded outlet under a license.
ww.A customer of the brand who buys its pro: A customer buys the brand's products, while a franchisee is a business owner who pays for the right to operate an outlet under the brand's name and system.

rw: A franchisor is the company that owns a brand and licenses its name, products and business system to franchisees, who pay fees and often royalties to use them.

ww.The bank that lends to the outlet owner: A bank that lends to the outlet owner is a lender, which is a different role from the franchisor that owns the brand and licenses its system.
ww.The person who runs the local outlet and: The person who runs the local outlet and pays a fee is the franchisee, not the franchisor, who grants the license and receives the fee.
ww.The customer who buys the product from t: The customer who buys the product from the outlet is a consumer, and has no role in owning or licensing the brand as a franchisor does.

rw: A royalty is a payment made to the owner of a brand, patent or creative work for the ongoing right to use it, often a share of sales.

ww.A fine for breaking a rule of the brand: A fine for breaking a rule is a penalty for misconduct, whereas a royalty is an agreed payment for the continuing use of someone's brand or idea.
ww.A tax on imported goods at the border po: A tax on imported goods at the border is a tariff or customs duty paid to the government, not a royalty paid to the owner of an idea.
ww.A payment for one-time labor made once a: A one time payment for labor after a job is done is a wage or fee, whereas a royalty keeps being paid as long as the brand or idea is used.

rw: Entrepreneurs start new businesses, which creates jobs, brings new products and ideas to market, and helps drive competition and growth in an economy.

ww.Printing the nation's money supply: Printing the nation's money supply is done by the central bank and the treasury, not by entrepreneurs, whose role is starting and growing new businesses.
ww.Setting official prices for all goods: Setting official prices for goods is price control by a government, while entrepreneurs operate in markets where prices come from supply and demand.
ww.Collecting income taxes from workers: Collecting income taxes from workers is a task for tax authorities, whereas entrepreneurs create firms and jobs, which indirectly generate the income that gets taxed.

rw: The Federal Trade Commission enforces federal rules on unfair and deceptive practices, including false advertising, and can order firms to stop and pay penalties.

ww.The Social Security Agency: The Social Security Agency pays retirement and disability benefits and does not police advertising claims, so it does not enforce rules against false advertising.
ww.The Federal Reserve Board: The Federal Reserve Board sets monetary policy and supervises banks, and it has no job enforcing federal rules against deceptive advertising by businesses.
ww.The Bureau of Labor Statistics: The Bureau of Labor Statistics collects data on jobs, wages and prices; it is a statistics agency with no power to enforce advertising rules.

rw: The SEC requires public companies to file regular, accurate financial disclosures so investors can judge the firm, and it can punish fraud and misleading reports.

ww.Fixed prices for their products sold: The SEC does not set product prices, because prices come from markets, and its role is to protect investors by requiring honest information from public companies.
ww.Hiring a set number of new workers: The SEC does not tell companies how many workers to hire, as hiring is a management decision, and its rules focus on investor information and fair markets.
ww.A guaranteed profit each year for firms: No agency can guarantee a profit each year to firms, since profit depends on market conditions, and the SEC only requires honest reporting, not results.

rw: Deregulation means the government reduces or removes rules that apply to an industry, often to encourage competition, lower costs and give firms more freedom to operate.

ww.Taxing an industry far more heavily than: Taxing an industry far more heavily is a tax increase, not deregulation, which removes or relaxes government rules instead of adding financial burdens.
ww.Taking over an industry entirely by the: Taking over an industry entirely by the state is nationalization, which increases government control, whereas deregulation reduces the rules that apply to an industry.
ww.Adding more rules to an industry for str: Adding more rules for stricter standards is regulation, or re-regulation, and it is the opposite of deregulation, which reduces the rules a government imposes.

rw: Firms often ignore the costs of pollution that fall on other people, called negative externalities, so regulation makes them account for the damage they cause.

ww.Clean air is a private good for each per: Clean air is a public good that people share and cannot be easily excluded from, not a private good, and this is why markets alone struggle to protect it.
ww.Pollution raises company profit for ever: Pollution does not raise profit for everyone; it imposes costs on third parties, and the harm to society is the main reason regulation is argued for.
ww.Markets always price pollution correctly: Markets do not always price pollution correctly, because polluters do not pay for the harm to others, and this market failure is what regulation targets.

rw: A carbon tax makes polluters pay for the harm their emissions cause, turning an outside cost into a price they must weigh, which pushes them to pollute less.

ww.Remove all costs from firms in the marke: A carbon tax does not remove costs from firms; it adds a cost to emitting carbon so that firms have a reason to cut their emissions.
ww.Ban all production of energy for good: A carbon tax raises the cost of emitting carbon but does not ban energy production, and firms may keep producing if they pay the tax.
ww.Reward firms that pollute with extra emi: Rewarding polluters with extra emissions is the opposite of a carbon tax, which penalizes emissions by charging a tax on each unit of carbon released.

rw: A tradable pollution permit gives a firm the right to emit a set amount, and firms can buy or sell permits, so total pollution stays under a cap.

ww.A free pass to pollute without limit whe: A pass to pollute without limit would defeat the purpose, since permits set a cap on emissions and each permit allows only a fixed quantity.
ww.A fine for emitting any pollution into t: A fine for emitting pollution is a penalty, not a permit; a permit is an allowance to emit a set amount that can be traded between firms.
ww.A ban on all emissions from any firm in: A ban on all emissions would stop production completely, whereas permits allow limited pollution under a cap and let firms trade the right to emit.

rw: National defense is a public good that protects everyone at once; one person's protection does not reduce another's, and nobody can easily be excluded from it.

ww.A designer jacket: A designer jacket is a private good that individuals buy for themselves, and sellers can exclude those who do not pay, so it is not a public good.
ww.A restaurant meal: A restaurant meal is a private good that only the buyer consumes, and the restaurant can refuse service to anyone who does not pay for it.
ww.A concert ticket: A concert ticket is a private good because only ticket holders can attend, so non payers are excluded, which means it is not a public good.

rw: Vaccination gives benefits to others by reducing the spread of disease, so society gains more than the buyer alone, and a subsidy raises vaccination toward the best level.

ww.Vaccines cost nothing to make, so price: Vaccines cost real money to make, so the claim that they cost nothing is false; the subsidy exists because society gains from vaccination beyond what buyers get.
ww.Vaccines harm third parties in the marke: Vaccines protect third parties by cutting disease spread, so they create benefits to others rather than harm, which is why a subsidy is used and not a tax.
ww.Markets over-supply vaccines to all buye: Markets tend to under supply vaccines because buyers ignore the benefit to others, so a claim of over supply gets the direction of the problem backward.

rw: An excise tax on tobacco raises revenue for the government and also raises the price of cigarettes, which discourages use, especially among price sensitive buyers and young people.

ww.Lower the price for all buyers: An excise tax on tobacco raises the price for buyers, not lowers it, and the goal is to discourage use while collecting revenue.
ww.Encourage smoking to raise revenue: Encouraging smoking is the opposite of public health goals; the tax raises the price of tobacco so that fewer people smoke while bringing in government revenue.
ww.Replace all income taxes soon: An excise tax on one product cannot replace all income taxes, since tobacco sales are far too small to fund the whole government budget.

rw: A user fee is a charge paid by those who use a particular government service, such as a park entrance fee or a toll, so users help fund it.

ww.A loan from the state to a firm or perso: A loan from the state to a firm or person is credit that must be repaid, and a user fee is a charge for using a service.
ww.A fine for breaking the law or a rule: A fine for breaking the law is a penalty for wrongdoing, whereas a user fee is a price for using a government service legally.
ww.A tax paid by every citizen each year: A tax paid by every citizen each year is a general tax, while a user fee is paid only by people who actually use a service.

rw: The FTC reviews mergers that might reduce competition and can challenge or block them, so that consumers are protected from higher prices and fewer choices.

ww.Forces all firms to merge into one compa: The FTC does not force firms to merge; it checks proposed mergers and can challenge those that harm competition, which is the opposite of forcing combinations.
ww.Sets the price of merged firms' goods ea: The FTC does not set the price of merged firms' goods, because prices are set by firms in markets, and its role is to review deals for competition effects.
ww.Approves every merger without any review: The FTC does review mergers and may block or set conditions on them, so saying it approves every merger without any review is plainly false.

rw: The Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 was passed to break up monopolies and ban price fixing and other practices that restrain trade and reduce competition.

ww.Set the minimum wage for all workers: The minimum wage is set by other laws, such as the Fair Labor Standards Act, and the Sherman Act has nothing to do with worker pay.
ww.Regulate food labels on packaged goods: Food labeling is regulated by laws such as the Food and Drug Act and later labeling laws, which came well after and differ from the Sherman Act.
ww.Create the income tax for the government: The income tax was created by other laws and the Sixteenth Amendment, while the Sherman Act focused on competition and had no role in creating a tax.

rw: A patent gives an inventor exclusive rights to make, use and sell an invention for a set period, commonly twenty years in the United States.

ww.Exclusive rights to a brand name or a lo: Exclusive rights to a brand name or logo are called a trademark, which is a different kind of intellectual property from a patent on an invention.
ww.Exclusive rights to a book, song or film: Exclusive rights to a book, song or film are called a copyright, which lasts for the author's life plus years, and it is not a patent.
ww.A license to open a store in a town or c: A license to open a store in a town is a local business permit, whereas a patent protects an invention and has nothing to do with store openings.

rw: A patent lets only the holder sell the invention for a set time, which gives a temporary monopoly that rewards the inventor before competitors can copy it.

ww.Patents set price ceilings by law for go: Patents do not set price ceilings; they grant exclusive rights, and the holder is free to set the price, which can be high during the protected period.
ww.Patents let any firm copy the invention: If any firm could copy the invention at any time, there would be no exclusive right, so a patent does the opposite of allowing free copying.
ww.Patents end all competition permanently: Patents expire after a fixed term, so they cannot end competition permanently, and after expiry other firms may copy the invention and compete freely.

rw: A copyright is the legal right of a creator to control the copying and distribution of an original work, such as a book, song, film or software.

ww.A guarantee of a work's quality given to: A guarantee of quality is a warranty given by a seller, while a copyright protects the creator's right to control copies of an original work.
ww.A license to sell goods abroad for a fir: A license to sell goods abroad is an export license, which is a trade permit and has no link to protecting an original creative work.
ww.A tax on creative workers such as author: A copyright is not a tax on creative workers; it is a legal protection that benefits authors and artists by controlling who may copy their work.

rw: The Fair Labor Standards Act sets the federal minimum wage and requires overtime pay, usually one and a half times pay beyond forty hours a week.

ww.Bank deposit insurance: Bank deposit insurance is provided by the FDIC under banking law, and it is separate from the Fair Labor Standards Act, which covers wages and hours.
ww.Stock market trading rules: Stock market trading rules come from the securities laws and the SEC, not the Fair Labor Standards Act, which covers pay and hours of employees.
ww.Product safety labels: Product safety labels are covered by consumer protection laws and agencies, whereas the Fair Labor Standards Act deals with employee wages, hours and child labor.

rw: The Occupational Safety and Health Act aims to keep workplaces safe and healthy by setting standards, requiring employers to fix hazards, and allowing inspections by OSHA.

ww.Guarantee all job promotions: No law can guarantee job promotions, which depend on performance and employer decisions, and the Occupational Safety and Health Act deals with workplace safety instead.
ww.Limit the number of workers hired: The Act does not limit how many workers a firm hires; it sets safety and health standards that apply to workplaces whatever the size of the staff.
ww.Set the price of insurance cover: Setting the price of insurance cover is not what the Act does; its purpose is to make workplaces safe and healthy through standards and inspections.

rw: The ADA requires employers to provide reasonable accommodations for qualified workers with disabilities, such as changes to equipment or schedules, unless it causes undue hardship.

ww.Closing offices that lack ramps and lift: The Americans with Disabilities Act does not close offices lacking ramps; it requires reasonable accommodations and removal of barriers where this can be done without undue hardship.
ww.Paying disabled workers more than all ot: The ADA bans discrimination and does not require paying disabled workers more than others; they must be paid on the same basis as comparable workers.
ww.Hiring only workers with disabilities fo: The ADA does not require hiring only workers with disabilities; it forbids discrimination against qualified people and says nothing about reserving all openings for them.

rw: A government contract is an agreement in which a firm supplies goods or services to the government, such as building a road or providing equipment, for a set payment.

ww.A license to operate a business in a sta: A license to operate a business in a state is a permit issued by authorities, which differs from a contract where a firm agrees to supply the government.
ww.A subsidy paid to households to help pay: A subsidy paid to households for food and housing is a transfer payment or welfare benefit, not an agreement for a firm to supply the government.
ww.A tax form for firms that sell goods to: A tax form for firms selling to the state is a filing document, while a government contract is the agreement under which the firm supplies goods or services.

rw: Government purchases are one component of GDP, along with consumption, investment and net exports, so they count as part of total spending on output.

ww.They are ignored in the GDP figures: Government purchases are not ignored; they are counted in GDP as the G in the expenditure formula, since the government buys goods and services too.
ww.They only affect imports of goods: Government purchases affect more than imports, because they are spending on domestic output, and they directly add to GDP as one part of total spending.
ww.They are subtracted from the GDP total: Government purchases are added to GDP, not subtracted, because they are spending on newly produced goods and services, such as roads, schools and defense.

rw: The multiplier effect means a round of government spending becomes income for others, who spend part of it again, so total output can rise by more than the original amount.

ww.Spending equals the tax collected, so th: The multiplier effect is not about balancing the budget; it describes how spending is re-spent through the economy, and it does not require taxes to equal spending.
ww.Spending has no effect on income or outp: Government spending does affect income and output, since recipients earn money and spend it, so the claim that it has no effect at all is wrong.
ww.Spending always lowers output in the eco: Spending does not always lower output; the multiplier works in the opposite direction, raising output by more than the first round of spending would suggest.

rw: The federal minimum wage sets a legal floor under pay, so employers covered by the law cannot pay less than that hourly amount to covered workers.

ww.Guarantee full employment for all: A minimum wage cannot guarantee full employment, because it sets a pay floor but does not create jobs, and some argue it can reduce them.
ww.Cap how much any worker can earn: The minimum wage is a floor, not a ceiling, so it does not cap how much a worker can earn; workers may be paid more than it.
ww.Replace all collective bargaining: The minimum wage does not replace collective bargaining, because unions still negotiate pay and conditions above the legal floor for their members.

rw: A tariff raises the price of imported goods, so domestic producers face less competition from abroad, which shields them and lets them sell more or charge more.

ww.It exposes them to more foreign competit: A tariff raises the price of imports, which lowers foreign competition for domestic producers, so saying it exposes them to more competition gets the effect backward.
ww.It bans them from exporting goods abroad: A tariff taxes imported goods and does not restrict a country's own exports, so it does not ban domestic producers from selling goods abroad.
ww.It sets their prices by law for each goo: A tariff is a tax on imports and does not set domestic producers' prices by law, since those firms remain free to set their own prices.

rw: A quota limits the quantity of an import, which reduces supply, and with demand unchanged the price of the imported good tends to rise.

ww.It becomes zero: A quota limits supply and does not make the price zero; a price of zero would mean the good is free, which cannot result from restricting quantity.
ww.It tends to fall: A quota cuts the supply of the imported good, and less supply with the same demand pushes the price up, not down, so falling prices is wrong.
ww.It stays pegged: A quota does not peg the price to a fixed level; it limits quantity, and the market price still moves, rising when supply is restricted.

rw: Nationalization is the government taking ownership of a private industry or firm, so that the state owns and often runs it, sometimes with compensation to owners.

ww.A firm selling shares to the public for: A firm selling shares to the public for the first time is an initial public offering, which changes ownership but does not move a private industry into government hands.
ww.A firm merging with a competitor from ab: A firm merging with a foreign competitor is an international merger between private companies, and the government does not take ownership of it.
ww.A firm moving to another country to avoi: A firm moving to another country is relocation, often called offshoring, and the government does not take ownership of any industry in doing so.

rw: Privatization means selling government owned assets or enterprises to private owners, which moves ownership and often operation of a business from the state to the private sector.

ww.A firm going out of business for good th: A firm going out of business is a closure or bankruptcy, which ends the company rather than moving government owned assets into private hands.
ww.A firm hiding its profits from the tax o: A firm hiding profits from the tax office is tax evasion, which is illegal, and it has no connection with selling government owned assets to private owners.
ww.The state taking over a private firm and: The state taking over and running a private firm is nationalization, which is the opposite of privatization, where the government sells or hands over assets.

rw: Real GDP adjusts for changes in the price level, using constant prices from a base year, so that a rise in GDP shows more output and not just higher prices.

ww.Changes in tax rates paid: Real GDP does not adjust for tax rates; it removes the effect of price changes so that output in different years can be compared fairly.
ww.Changes in exchange rates: Exchange rates affect trade values but real GDP does not adjust for them; it adjusts for the price level using a base year's prices.
ww.Changes in population size: Population size is not part of the real GDP adjustment; adjusting for population gives GDP per capita, which is a different measure from real GDP.

rw: Real GDP growth is roughly nominal growth minus inflation, so 6% minus 2% gives about 4%, showing that output rose by 4% after removing the price effect.

ww.8%: An 8% figure comes from adding 6% and 2%, but inflation must be subtracted from nominal growth to find real growth, so 8% is wrong.
ww.12%: A 12% figure comes from multiplying 6% by 2, which has no meaning here; real growth is nominal growth minus inflation, not a product of the two.
ww.2%: A 2% figure is just the inflation rate and ignores the nominal growth, but real growth equals 6% minus 2%, which is more than 2%.

rw: The GDP deflator is a price index that covers all goods and services included in GDP, and it is used to convert nominal GDP into real GDP.

ww.A device that reduces unemployment in ci: A GDP deflator is not a device that reduces unemployment; it is a statistical measure of prices and has no power to change the labor market.
ww.A rule that caps inflation at a set leve: A rule capping inflation at a set level would be a policy or target, but the GDP deflator is just a measure of price changes, not a rule.
ww.A tool that lowers a firm's taxes by a s: A tool that lowers a firm's taxes is a tax measure, but the GDP deflator is a price index used to measure inflation across the economy.

rw: The Consumer Price Index tracks the prices of a basket of goods and services that households typically buy, and it is the main gauge of inflation for consumers.

ww.Wages paid to workers in all sectors of: Wages paid to workers are tracked by wage and earnings data, while the Consumer Price Index follows the prices households pay for a typical basket of goods.
ww.Prices producers get for goods sold to d: Prices producers receive for goods sold to dealers are tracked by the Producer Price Index, which is a different measure from the Consumer Price Index.
ww.Stock market values of large firms each: Stock market values are measured by stock indexes such as the S&P 500, whereas the CPI measures the cost of goods and services households buy.

rw: Inflation is the change in CPI divided by last year's CPI, so 260 minus 250 is 10, and 10 divided by 250 gives 0.04, or 4%.

ww.26%: A 26% figure takes the new CPI value as a percent, but inflation is the change divided by the old CPI, which here is 10 over 250.
ww.2.5%: A 2.5% figure divides the 10 point change by 400, which is not the right base; the base should be last year's CPI of 250, giving 4%.
ww.10%: A 10% figure uses the 10 point change as if it were a percent, but it must be divided by the old CPI of 250 to give 4%.

rw: Core inflation leaves out volatile food and energy prices, which swing with weather and oil markets, so policymakers can see the underlying inflation trend more clearly.

ww.It ignores all price changes in the econ: Core inflation does not ignore all price changes; it removes only the volatile food and energy prices so that the underlying trend in other prices is easier to see.
ww.It counts only food and energy prices to: Core inflation excludes food and energy prices instead of counting only them, so saying it counts only food and energy prices gets the definition reversed.
ww.It predicts stock prices by removing ene: Core inflation is a measure of price trends, not a tool for predicting stock prices, and removing energy does not give it that purpose.

rw: The labor force participation rate is the share of working age people who are either working or actively looking for work, out of the total working age population.

ww.The share of jobs that are full time in: The share of jobs that are full time describes job quality, not the participation rate, which looks at how many working age people are in the labor force.
ww.The share of workers who are unemployed: The share of workers who are unemployed in the labor force is the unemployment rate, which is a different measure from the participation rate.
ww.The share of workers in unions across th: The share of workers in unions is the union membership rate, which tells us about labor organization and not about how many people are in the labor force.

rw: If discouraged workers give up and leave the labor force, they are no longer counted as unemployed, so the unemployment rate can fall even though no new jobs appeared.

ww.Taxes rise on all workers in the nation: Tax increases on workers do not directly change how the unemployment rate is counted, and they would not make it fall without any new jobs appearing.
ww.Prices fall across the whole economy: Falling prices across the economy do not by themselves reduce the share of people counted as unemployed, and no new jobs means no direct fall.
ww.More people join the labor force to seek: More people joining the labor force to seek work raises the number of job seekers, which tends to push the unemployment rate up, not make it fall.

rw: Underemployment is when workers hold jobs below their skill level or work fewer hours than they want, so labor is not being fully used even though they have work.

ww.Workers earn more than expected, above w: Workers who earn more than expected is a positive outcome and not underemployment, which refers to people not fully using their skills or hours.
ww.Workers have no jobs at all in the whole: Having no jobs at all describes unemployment, while underemployment means people do have jobs but those jobs are below their skills or fewer hours than wanted.
ww.Workers retire early by choice well befo: Retiring early by choice is a decision to leave the labor force and does not describe workers who want more hours or better matched jobs.

rw: A leading indicator is a statistic that tends to change before the economy changes, such as new housing permits, so it can help forecast turning points.

ww.A statistic that tends to change only af: A statistic that changes only after the economy does is a lagging indicator, such as the unemployment rate, and not a leading indicator.
ww.A statistic made up by a leader of the f: A leading indicator is not a number made up by a firm's leader; it is a measured economic statistic whose changes tend to come before the economy's.
ww.A statistic that never changes over any: A statistic that never changes would have no information about the economy, so it cannot be an indicator, and leading indicators do change ahead of the economy.

rw: A coincident indicator moves with the economy at the same time, such as industrial production or employment, so it shows where the economy is now.

ww.A statistic that moves long after the ec: A statistic that moves long after the economy does is a lagging indicator, so it is not a coincident indicator, which moves at the same time.
ww.A statistic that moves before the econom: A statistic that moves before the economy does is a leading indicator, whereas a coincident indicator moves at the same time as the economy does.
ww.A statistic that has no timing link to t: A statistic with no timing link to the economy would not be an indicator at all, whereas a coincident indicator moves in step with the economy.

rw: The unemployment rate is generally a lagging indicator because firms hire or lay off workers only after the economy has already turned up or down.

ww.Stock prices each day: Stock prices are generally a leading indicator because they tend to move before the economy changes, as investors look ahead to future profits.
ww.New housing permits: New housing permits are generally a leading indicator because builders apply for permits before construction, which happens ahead of the economy's changes in activity.
ww.Consumer confidence: Consumer confidence is generally a leading indicator because households that feel hopeful or worried change their spending plans before the economy itself shifts.

rw: A rising consumer confidence index suggests households feel better about jobs and income, so they may spend more, which can lift demand and economic growth.

ww.Prices will fall for certain: Rising confidence does not guarantee that prices will fall; it signals optimism about the economy, which tends to raise spending, and that can push prices up.
ww.Unemployment must be rising: Rising consumer confidence suggests households feel secure about jobs and income, so it does not point to rising unemployment, which would lower confidence instead.
ww.Households may spend less: When confidence rises, households feel better about the future and tend to spend more, not less, so predicting reduced spending reverses the usual relationship.

rw: The Index of Leading Economic Indicators combines several data series to signal turning points in the business cycle, such as upcoming peaks and troughs, before they occur.

ww.Count the firms in the economy each mont: Counting the firms in the economy is a business census task and not the aim of the Index of Leading Economic Indicators, which forecasts changes in activity.
ww.Measure the national debt in the economy: The national debt is measured by the Treasury from government borrowing records, and it is not what the Index of Leading Economic Indicators tries to measure.
ww.Set the interest rate for the whole econ: Interest rates are set by the central bank and by markets, not by an index, since the Index of Leading Economic Indicators only gives forecasting signals.

rw: A trade deficit occurs when the value of a country's imports is greater than the value of its exports over a period, so it buys more than it sells abroad.

ww.A fall in the exchange rate level: A fall in the exchange rate is a depreciation of the currency, which is different from a trade deficit, defined as imports exceeding exports.
ww.Government spending above revenue: Government spending above revenue is a budget deficit, which is a different concept from the trade deficit that compares imports with exports.
ww.Exports exceeding imports in value: Exports exceeding imports in value is a trade surplus, which is the opposite of a trade deficit, where imports are the larger amount.

rw: The trade balance is exports minus imports, so 400 minus 450 equals negative 50, which is a deficit of 50 billion dollars.

ww.A surplus of $50 billion: A surplus needs exports to exceed imports, but here exports of 400 are below imports of 450, so the balance is negative and not a surplus.
ww.A zero balance, no deficit: A zero balance would require exports and imports to be equal, but 400 billion is not equal to 450 billion, so there is a gap of 50.
ww.A deficit of $850 billion: The figure 850 billion comes from adding exports and imports together, but the trade balance is found by subtracting imports from exports, which gives a deficit of 50.

rw: The current account measures a country's trade in goods and services plus income flows and transfers with the rest of the world, so it shows its net external position.

ww.The number of firms in the country at a: The number of firms in a country is a business count and has nothing to do with the current account, which tracks flows of trade and income.
ww.The money in a person's checking account: Money in a person's checking account is a personal bank balance, while the current account is a national measure of trade and income flows with other countries.
ww.The country's yearly budget for all publ: A country's yearly budget for public services is a government spending plan, not the current account, which records international trade, income and transfers.

rw: In a recession, incomes, profits and spending fall, so the income, corporate and sales taxes collected typically fall, and this is called an automatic stabilizer effect.

ww.It stays unchanged: Tax revenue does not stay unchanged in a recession, because incomes and spending fall and so do income and sales tax receipts for the government.
ww.It rises sharply: A recession lowers incomes and sales, so tax revenue falls rather than rises sharply, and a sharp rise would be typical of strong growth.
ww.It turns into zero: Tax revenue falls in a recession but does not drop to zero, since people and firms still earn income and make purchases that are taxed.

rw: A yield curve compares interest rates on bonds, usually government bonds, with different maturities, and its shape helps show what investors expect for the economy.

ww.Profits of different firms across the ec: Profits of different firms are compared in company reports, whereas a yield curve compares interest rates on bonds that differ by their time to maturity.
ww.Wages in different cities across the cou: Wages in different cities are compared in labor market data, and a yield curve has nothing to do with wages or city differences.
ww.Prices of different brands of the same p: Prices of different brands of the same product are compared by shoppers, but a yield curve plots bond interest rates against time to maturity.

rw: An inverted yield curve, with short term rates above long term rates, has often come before recessions, so it signals a higher chance of a coming recession.

ww.A coming boom in output and sales: A coming boom is typically linked to a normal upward sloping yield curve, whereas an inverted curve has often come before slowdowns and not before booms.
ww.An end to inflation as prices stop risin: An inverted curve does not mean inflation is ending; it means short term rates are above long term rates, which has often come before a recession.
ww.No change in the economy for years: An inverted yield curve points to a possible change in the economy, because short term rates exceed long term rates, so it does not signal years of no change.

rw: The personal savings rate is the share of disposable income that households save instead of spend, which shows how much of their income they set aside.

ww.The share of spending on housing and foo: The share of spending on housing and food describes a spending pattern, whereas the savings rate measures the part of disposable income that is saved.
ww.The share of income paid in taxes each y: The share of income paid in taxes is the tax rate, but the personal savings rate looks at what households keep after taxes and do not spend.
ww.The interest rate on savings accounts at: The interest rate on savings accounts is what banks pay depositors, which is different from the savings rate, the share of income households save.

rw: Retail sales data shows how much consumers are spending at stores, which is a key sign of consumer demand and so of the strength of the economy.

ww.How many stores close each year in the n: Store closings are tracked in business closure data, but retail sales data measures the dollar value of what consumers spend at stores.
ww.How many workers stores hire each year: How many workers stores hire is employment data, while retail sales data measures the spending that consumers do at stores.
ww.How much stores pay in rent each month: Rent paid by stores is a cost of business, and retail sales data tracks revenue from consumer purchases, not stores' costs.

rw: The PMI is based on surveys of purchasing managers and gauges the health of manufacturing and service activity, with a reading above 50 showing expansion.

ww.The average wage of workers across the n: The average wage of workers is measured in earnings data, while the PMI is a survey based index on business activity in manufacturing and services.
ww.The number of banks in the whole country: The number of banks in a country is a count from banking regulators, and it is not what the Purchasing Managers' Index is designed to gauge.
ww.The price of homes in the whole country,: The price of homes is measured by house price indexes, whereas the PMI gauges business activity in manufacturing and services based on manager surveys.

rw: A tariff is a tax placed on imports, which raises their price, while a quota is a limit on the quantity of a good that can be imported.

ww.A tariff limits imports while a quota ta: This reverses the definitions, because a tariff is a tax on imports and a quota is a limit on the quantity of imports.
ww.Both mean the same thing in the law of t: The two are not the same, since a tariff raises government revenue through a tax and a quota caps quantities, so their effects differ.
ww.Both pay exporters directly in cash each: Neither tariffs nor quotas pay exporters in cash; both restrict imports, and a payment to exporters would instead describe an export subsidy.

rw: An export subsidy is government support, such as payments or tax breaks, that lowers the cost of exports, so the goods can be sold cheaper in foreign markets.

ww.A fine for exporters who break the trade: A fine for exporters who break trade rules is a penalty for violations, while an export subsidy is a support payment that helps exporters.
ww.A ban on exports of all goods and servic: A ban on exports of all goods is an export embargo, which stops exporting, whereas an export subsidy encourages more exporting by cutting the cost.
ww.A tax on exports of all goods and servic: A tax on exports is an export duty, which makes exports more costly, whereas an export subsidy lowers the cost and so is the opposite.

rw: Economists oppose export subsidies because they distort trade by artificially lowering export prices, and taxpayers must fund them, which wastes resources and can harm other countries.

ww.They lower prices at home and help all: Export subsidies lower prices for foreign buyers, not for people at home, and taxpayers pay for them, so the claim that they help all is wrong.
ww.They always raise efficiency in trade: Export subsidies do not always raise efficiency, because they push production toward goods that may not be made at lowest cost, so the word always is wrong.
ww.They remove all trade barriers for good: Export subsidies add a distortion to trade and do not remove barriers, so they do not lead to freer trade and may invite retaliation.

rw: Comparative advantage means countries gain by specializing in and trading goods they produce at lower opportunity cost, so total output and consumption can rise for all.

ww.One country gains only at another's expe: Trade is not a contest where one gains only at the other's expense; comparative advantage shows both countries can gain when each specializes where its opportunity cost is lower.
ww.All countries must make every good they: Comparative advantage says countries need not make every good at home, because they can specialize and trade, which lets them consume more than they could alone.
ww.Trade removes the need for specializatio: Trade depends on specialization, since countries focus on goods with lower opportunity cost, so saying trade removes the need for specialization is the opposite of the truth.

rw: Country X gives up 2 tools for 4 shirts, or 0.5 tool per shirt, while Y gives up 1 tool per shirt, so X has the lower cost.

ww.Country Y: Country Y gives up 1 tool per shirt, which is a higher opportunity cost than Country X, which gives up only half a tool, so Y does not hold the advantage.
ww.Both equally: The two countries have different opportunity costs of 0.5 and 1 tool per shirt, so they are not equal, and one of them has the advantage.
ww.Neither: One of the two countries must have the comparative advantage in shirts when opportunity costs differ, and here X gives up 0.5 tool per shirt and Y gives up 1.

rw: A trade surplus means exports are greater than imports, so net exports, equal to exports minus imports, are positive, which adds to a country's GDP.

ww.They are always zero: A surplus means exports exceed imports, so net exports, which are exports minus imports, are positive, not zero, in that case, and are not always zero.
ww.They are not measured: Net exports are measured and published in national accounts as a part of GDP, so saying they are not measured is false.
ww.They are negative: Negative net exports would mean imports exceed exports, which describes a trade deficit, not a surplus, so negative is the wrong sign for a surplus.

rw: A floating exchange rate is set by supply and demand for currencies in the foreign exchange market, so its value moves up and down as conditions change.

ww.A rate set by a company or private firm: A rate set by a private firm is not a floating exchange rate, because floating rates are determined by supply and demand in currency markets, not by any one company.
ww.A rate fixed by the government against a: A rate fixed by the government against another currency is a pegged or fixed exchange rate, which is the opposite of a floating rate.
ww.A rate that never changes over any perio: A floating exchange rate moves with supply and demand in currency markets, so it changes often, and saying it never changes is false.

rw: A fixed or pegged exchange rate is one that a government or central bank holds at a set value against another currency, often by buying or selling currency.

ww.A rate that changes every minute in mark: A rate that changes every minute in markets is a floating exchange rate, which responds to supply and demand, and is not fixed or pegged.
ww.A rate set by market forces and demand: A rate set by market forces and demand is a floating rate, while a pegged rate is held at a set value by the government.
ww.A rate set by tourists who travel abroad: Tourists do not set exchange rates, as their currency exchange is a small part of the market, and a pegged rate is set by the government.

rw: When demand for the euro rises relative to supply, buyers bid up its price against other currencies, so the euro appreciates and its value goes up.

ww.It becomes useless: Higher demand for the euro makes it more valuable, not useless, because buyers must bid more for it, and a currency with strong demand does not lose all value.
ww.It depreciates: Depreciation means a currency loses value, but a rise in demand relative to supply makes the euro worth more, which is the opposite effect.
ww.It stays frozen: In a floating system the price moves in response to supply and demand, so the euro would not stay frozen when demand rises above supply.

rw: A weaker home currency means foreign buyers need less of their own money to buy the home country's goods, so exports become cheaper for foreign buyers.

ww.Impossible to sell abroad: A weaker home currency does not make exports impossible to sell; it lowers their price abroad, so they tend to sell more, not less.
ww.Free of any tariffs abroad: Tariffs are set by importing countries and do not disappear when a currency weakens; a weaker currency changes the price in foreign currency, not tariff status.
ww.Pricier for foreign buyers: Pricier exports would result from a stronger home currency, not a weaker one, because foreign buyers would need more of their own money to buy the goods.

rw: The World Bank mainly finances development projects in poorer countries, such as infrastructure, health and education, through loans and grants, to help reduce poverty.

ww.Enforcing trade rules between all nation: Enforcing trade rules between nations is the job of the World Trade Organization, not the World Bank, which focuses on lending for development.
ww.Regulating world stock markets and share: The World Bank does not regulate stock markets or share prices; national regulators and exchanges do that, and the Bank funds development projects instead.
ww.Setting global interest rates for banks: Setting global interest rates is not a World Bank role, since central banks set their own rates and the Bank focuses on development finance.

rw: The International Monetary Fund supports monetary cooperation among countries and lends to those in financial trouble, such as balance of payments crises, often with policy conditions attached.

ww.Builds roads and schools in poorer count: Building roads and schools in poorer countries is more like the work of the World Bank, which funds development, while the IMF focuses on monetary stability.
ww.Collects tariffs for all nations and pay: The IMF does not collect tariffs for all nations or pay money out to poorer countries; tariffs are collected by each country's own customs service.
ww.Sets product standards for goods traded: Setting product standards for traded goods is work done by standards bodies and trade organizations, not the IMF, which deals with money and finance.

rw: The EU single market allows the free movement of goods, services, people and capital among member states, so businesses and workers can operate across borders easily.

ww.A market that is closed to all trade wit: A single market is open, not closed to trade with other nations, and it removes barriers among member states so trade flows freely between them.
ww.A market with no rules and no regulation: The single market has common rules and regulations that all members follow, so saying it has no rules of any kind is false.
ww.A market limited to one country, in whic: A single market covers many member countries, not one, and goods cross borders freely within it, so a market where goods may not cross a border is wrong.

rw: The USMCA is a trade agreement among the United States, Mexico and Canada that replaced NAFTA and sets rules for trade, labor and digital commerce.

ww.A banking union among nations in Africa: The USMCA is not a banking union and does not involve Africa or the Middle East; its members are in North America only.
ww.A tax treaty with many countries in Asia: The USMCA is a trade agreement within North America, not a tax treaty with Asian and Pacific countries, which are not members of the pact.
ww.A military pact in Europe between nation: The USMCA is about trade and not defense, and its members are in North America, so a military pact among European nations is incorrect.

rw: In a customs union, members drop tariffs on trade among themselves and apply one shared tariff on goods from outside, which keeps outside trade treatment consistent.

ww.Members ban all trade among themselves a: A customs union does not ban trade among its members; it removes tariffs among them, so banning all trade is the opposite of what it does.
ww.Members keep separate tariffs for each o: In a customs union members do not keep separate outside tariffs; they adopt a common external tariff, so the claim of separate outside rates is wrong.
ww.Members share a single currency only, an: A single currency is a feature of a monetary union and not the defining feature of a customs union, which concerns tariffs on trade among members.

rw: A trade war is when countries raise tariffs on each other's goods in turn, as each side retaliates, which usually raises prices and cuts trade.

ww.A dispute inside a single company over w: A dispute inside a single company over wages is a labor dispute, while a trade war is a conflict between countries over trade barriers.
ww.A fight with weapons over trade routes b: A trade war uses tariffs and trade barriers, not weapons, so a fight over trade routes with weapons is a military conflict and not a trade war.
ww.A festival of imports and exports held e: A festival of imports and exports is not a trade war; the term describes escalating tariffs and retaliation between countries, which harm trade and not celebrate it.

rw: Dumping is selling goods in a foreign market below their cost or below the price charged at home, which can harm local producers and may lead to duties.

ww.Selling goods at a fair price abroad, th: Selling at a fair price abroad, equal to the home price, is normal trade, whereas dumping means selling below cost or below the home price.
ww.Throwing away unsold goods at the end of: Throwing away unsold goods is waste disposal, and dumping in trade refers to selling goods abroad at unfairly low prices, not discarding them.
ww.Giving products to charity at no cost to: Giving products to charity is a donation, not dumping, which is a pricing practice in export markets where goods are sold below cost or home price.

rw: The infant industry argument says new industries need temporary protection, such as tariffs, until they grow large enough and learn enough to compete with established foreign firms.

ww.Old industries must be shut down at once: The argument is about protecting new industries and not about shutting down old ones, and it does not call for old industries to be closed by law.
ww.Babies need protection from imports of t: The infant industry argument is about young industries in a country, not babies, and it concerns tariffs and not protection of toys or children.
ww.All industries should be taxed more heav: The infant industry argument calls for protecting new industries, not taxing all industries more heavily, so taxing all industries every year does not fit the argument.

rw: A common criticism is that protection may last too long, so the industry never has to improve and inefficient firms stay alive at consumers' expense.

ww.It forces firms to export more goods to: The argument calls for protecting new industries from imports and does not force firms to export more, so forcing exports is not a criticism of it.
ww.It removes all costs for consumers, as f: Keeping out foreign goods does not remove costs for consumers; it often raises prices and narrows choice, but the claim that it removes all costs is wrong.
ww.It always lowers prices forever for all: Protection does not always lower prices forever; it tends to raise them, so claiming it always lowers prices is not a true criticism of the argument.

rw: A multinational enterprise is a firm that operates in several countries, with offices, factories or stores in more than one nation, and often a home base.

ww.A government trade office in the capital: A government trade office in the capital is a public agency, whereas a multinational enterprise is a private firm that runs operations in several countries.
ww.A union of workers across borders and tr: A union of workers across borders is a labor organization, but a multinational enterprise is a business firm that operates in more than one country.
ww.A firm limited to one city or one town: A firm limited to one city or one town operates locally, which is the opposite of a multinational firm that has operations in many countries.

rw: Globalization often brings cheaper goods for consumers but can cause job losses in industries that cannot compete with imports, which is a real trade-off for workers.

ww.No change in jobs or prices for anyone i: Globalization changes prices and jobs for many people, so claiming no change in jobs or prices for anyone in any industry ignores the real trade-off.
ww.Lower wages for every worker without exc: Globalization does not lower wages for every worker without exception, because some workers in export industries gain, so the word every makes the claim false.
ww.Higher prices and more jobs for everyone: Globalization usually lowers prices through competition and does not give higher prices and more jobs for everyone, so that claim is the wrong way round.

rw: A trade-off means giving up one thing in order to get another, since resources are limited and choosing one option usually means passing up an alternative.

ww.Getting everything wanted at no cost: Getting everything wanted at no cost ignores scarcity, because resources are limited, and a trade-off exists exactly because choices have costs.
ww.Trading only with other countries: A trade-off is a choice between alternatives, not trade with other countries, so trading only with other countries is a narrower idea than the term means.
ww.Selling goods for a higher price: Selling goods for a higher price is a pricing decision, whereas a trade-off is about giving up one option to gain another.

rw: The opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up, which is the pay from the shift the student did not work while studying on Saturday.

ww.The cost of the textbooks bought: The cost of textbooks is an out of pocket expense, but the opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative, which here is the paid shift.
ww.The time spent studying only: Time spent studying is what the student chose to do, not what was given up; the opportunity cost is the pay from the shift not worked.
ww.Nothing, because studying is free: Studying is not free, because the student gives up the pay from a shift, so saying the cost is nothing ignores opportunity cost.

rw: A production possibilities frontier is a curve showing the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its resources and technology when it uses them fully.

ww.A map of trade routes used by cargo ship: A map of trade routes for ships shows shipping paths and has no link to the production possibilities frontier, which is a graph of output choices.
ww.A tax schedule listing the rates for eac: A tax schedule lists rates for income levels, which is a government fiscal tool, whereas the production possibilities frontier shows the output an economy can make.
ww.A list of the profits of each company fo: A list of company profits is a financial record, and it does not show combinations of goods an economy can make, which is what the frontier shows.

rw: A point inside the production possibilities frontier shows that the economy is not using all its resources fully, so there is unused capacity or inefficiency.

ww.An impossible output for the economy: A point inside the frontier is attainable, so it is not impossible; impossible output lies outside the frontier, beyond what resources allow.
ww.Rapid growth in the whole economy: A point inside the frontier shows output below capacity, so it does not show rapid growth, which would appear as the frontier shifting outward over time.
ww.Full efficiency of resources: Full efficiency of resources is shown by points on the frontier, not inside it, because a point inside means resources could produce more.

rw: Economic growth increases resources or improves technology, so the economy can produce more of both goods, and the frontier shifts outward to show it.

ww.Turns it into a line: Economic growth does not turn the frontier into a line; the frontier keeps its shape but moves outward when the economy can produce more.
ww.Shifts it inward: Shifting the frontier inward would mean the economy can produce less, as in a loss of resources, which is the opposite of economic growth.
ww.Removes it fully: Growth does not remove the frontier; every economy still faces limits on output, and the frontier simply moves outward as the limits expand.

rw: The law of demand says that as price rises, quantity demanded falls, other things equal, because higher prices push buyers toward substitutes or to buy less.

ww.Demand is always fixed at one level for: Demand is not fixed at one level; the law of demand says the quantity demanded changes as the price changes, so a fixed level for all prices is wrong.
ww.Price has no effect on demand for any go: Price does affect demand, since buyers respond to price changes, and the claim of no effect for any good contradicts the law of demand.
ww.As price rises, quantity demanded rises: The law of demand says quantity demanded falls as price rises, not rises, and buyers seeing quality in high prices is not the general rule.

rw: The law of supply says that as price rises, quantity supplied rises, other things equal, because higher prices make producing more profitable and attract more sellers.

ww.Supply never changes for any price level: Supply changes with price, since the law of supply links price and quantity supplied, so supply never changing is false.
ww.As price rises, quantity supplied falls,: The law of supply says quantity supplied rises with price, not falls, so the claim that sellers sell less when price rises states the opposite.
ww.Producers ignore prices when they plan t: Producers respond to prices, since higher prices make production more profitable, so saying they ignore prices when planning output contradicts the law of supply.

rw: A rise in consumer incomes raises demand for a normal good like pizza at every price, so the whole demand curve shifts to the right.

ww.A rise in the price of pizza: A rise in the price of pizza moves along the demand curve and lowers quantity demanded, but it does not shift the curve itself to the right.
ww.A drop in ingredient costs: A drop in ingredient costs affects supply, not demand, so it shifts the supply curve to the right and leaves the demand curve where it is.
ww.A fall in consumer incomes: A fall in consumer incomes reduces demand for a normal good such as pizza, which shifts the demand curve to the left, not the right.
